Everyone talks about AI in ready-made cards: every job will disappear, machines cannot be creative, hybrid systems always win. Nearly every card is dealt by a company with an interest in you playing it. Each week we turn one card over and dig one spade deeper into the I of AI: what intelligence actually is, and how a company, a team or a machine must be organised to get more of it. More about us, and about the cards, in About.

Issue #3  ·  14 Aug 2026

Why Every Citizen Should Invest in AMI

Yann LeCun raised 1.03 billion dollars in seed money, the largest seed round in European history, to argue that the entire industry is betting wrong. If he is right, intelligence is not a matter of scale, and the winner-takes-all story around AI collapses. We take his bet seriously, because it is also a bet that intelligence, like it always has been, stays distributed. That makes this a fight for every citizen, not just every investor.

On March 10, Emmanuel Macron congratulated Yann LeCun on X: "[...] This is the France of researchers, builders and the bold. Bravo!" The occasion: AMI, the AI lab LeCun had founded after leaving Meta, had just closed the largest seed round in European history: $1.03 billion, at a $3.5 billion valuation, with no product and no revenue.

To understand why Macron thinks this is a public matter, look at how the tech bros accumulated so much capital and power in a short time, and why AI companies are now the most valuable companies in the history of the world.

Tech companies get a double premium for scale. One: Most tech plays have huge fixed costs, creating very high barriers to entry. Two: As Brian Arthur showed, network plays show 'increasing returns'. Each new customer in a network adds more value than the last: the logic behind Whatsapp, Uber, and the rest of the Magnificent Seven.

So it's no coincidence that investors and tech bros frame AI also as a winner takes all game. They want us to believe that Anthropic and OpenAI are like Microsoft or Google; all about scale. And the scale is just in the compute. Throw more compute at it, and the machines get smarter. Richard Sutton's Bitter Lesson put it as follows: "general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective." Investors really want to believe that, which is why Nvidia became the fastest-rising stock in history.

This is the conviction LeCun is betting against. He spent twelve years at Meta, first as founding director of its FAIR lab, later as Chief AI Scientist, and shares the 2018 Turing Award for deep learning itself. He holds that the current view of AI cannot be right: a child, running on a 20-watt brain, learns things in minutes no language model has ever managed. A human needs about fifteen hours behind the wheel to earn a driver's license without crashing; a self-driving system needs to run off the road thousands of times before it learns what a mistake even is.

The alternative LeCun proposes is JEPA: Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture. A token-prediction model, like Claude or ChatGPT, guesses what comes next: the next word, the next pixel. A JEPA model instead builds an internal model of how things relate and behave, and predicts the underlying structure, not the exact outcome. A tennis player returning a serve isn't predicting the ball's exact position a second from now, she's predicting its trajectory. That's a world model: not a simulation of everything, but a compressed, useful model of how the world works.

Here's why this matters beyond the lab. Scale and increasing returns only produce concentration if intelligence is a matter of brute-force scale, where the winner is simply whoever owns the most compute. But human intelligence was never built that way: it's distributed across eight billion twenty-watt brains, none of which need a data center. Also, if the idea of world models is correct, perhaps systems will become specialized around certain knowledge or skill areas. Then much smaller players could enter the game successfully. If LeCun is right, the winner-takes-all story around AI collapses with it: the closest thing AI has to a revolution against a handful of companies owning the future of intelligence simply because they can afford the compute. Every citizen, not just every investor, has a reason to want him to be right. Betting on AMI isn't just a bet on an architecture. It's a bet that intelligence stays distributed.

Sources
LeCun: the working proof of a world model
LeCun, Maes, Le Lidec, Scieur and Balestriero, "LeWorldModel" on arXiv · 13 March 2026

Celebrated AI researcher Yann LeCun, who until recently worked at Meta, has been critical of the claims made about large language models for years. He finds them impressive, but points out that they don't resemble how humans learn in any meaningful way, and therefore will never lead to AGI. His favorite example: a human learns to drive safely in about fifteen hours, while the classic approach to self-driving cars needs the vehicle to run off the road thousands of times before it learns what a mistake even is. What's missing, according to LeCun, is a world model: an internal, abstract picture of how the world works and responds to actions, letting a system plan ahead without predicting every outcome pixel by pixel. In this March 2026 paper, LeCun builds on the vision he introduced in 2022, and delivers the working proof for the first time: a model that trains stably straight from raw camera footage, without the usual workarounds, and runs on a single ordinary GPU.

arxiv.org/abs/2603.19312
Kaplan: the scaling laws that set the industry's course
Kaplan et al. (OpenAI) on arXiv · January 2020

In January 2020, Kaplan and nine other OpenAI researchers, including Dario Amodei, published a paper that would set the course for the entire industry. They showed empirically that a language model's performance follows a predictable power law as you scale up three things: parameters, training data, and compute. The pattern holds across more than seven orders of magnitude, with no sign of leveling off. The evidence doesn't rest on a theoretical explanation of why this happens, just on the sheer regularity of the curve itself, startlingly straight lines on a log scale. This paper directly justified the decision to scale GPT-3 up to 175 billion parameters. It wasn't just a scientific position. It was ammunition for everyone who argued AI would become a winner-takes-all market, exactly the kind of scale-sensitive dynamic we discussed earlier.

arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361
Sutton: the bitter lesson of seventy years of AI
Richard Sutton, incompleteideas.net · March 2019

Richard Sutton is one of the founders of reinforcement learning. Together with his former doctoral advisor Andrew Barto, he shared the 2024 Turing Award for it, computing's highest honor. In his short, widely read essay The Bitter Lesson (2019), he draws a hard lesson from seventy years of AI research: whenever researchers built human knowledge and structure into their systems, it worked well at first, and was eventually beaten anyway by more general methods that simply used more compute and data. Intelligence, his argument goes, ultimately scales with compute, not with cleverer architecture. It isn't a universally accepted truth (LeCun is living proof of the opposite), but it is the dominant view at many of the largest AI labs, and the implicit justification behind every decision to just train a bigger model.

incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html
Craik: where the world model idea began
Kenneth Craik, The Nature of Explanation, Cambridge University Press · 1943

The term world model that LeCun uses traces back to Kenneth Craik, who published the book The Nature of Explanation in 1943. Craik was a kind of cybernetician avant la lettre (it was in cybernetics, after all, that the first major AI ideas took shape), and spent the war studying how pilots interact with cockpit instruments. The “small-scale models” he wrote about were, as so often, drawn from his own life: as a hobby, he built ships in bottles. His ideas about cognition rest on the same image: humans carry a small model of the world in their heads, and reason through a kind of parallel with that world, without ever having to live through the real events themselves. *Book, Cambridge University Press. No free-access link available.*

Issue #2  ·  7 Aug 2026

The leakage moved one level up

Everyone still asks which files are safe to upload in your AI application. That question is for enterprise users largely settled. The exposure that is left for the company, moved one level up. In what your architecture reveals about the way you work. This week: Karp's alarm about this level up, the remedy he does not mention, and why every warning Palantir sends out happens to sell a Palantir product.

Read this issue

In early July, Alex Karp of Palantir went on American television and accused the AI labs of theft. They are draining the value out of the enterprises that use them, he said. Most people who heard him, thought this was about file sharing. Which of my files are safe to upload in a prompt, or publish in any media. That was not his point.

So let me start with the worry Karp was not referring to. The original sin of the labs was training their models on the open internet without asking anyone. The courts have - surprisingly enough - mostly forgiven that sin. Training is fair use, as long as the material was obtained legally. The narrower crime, the training on pirated content, ended this summer in the largest copyright settlement ever written. Anthropic agreed to pay authors about three thousand dollars a work, a small fee to pay for the sin of the century.

Pamela Samuelson, who has shaped American copyright thinking for decades, sharpened her position. Copyright protects the now your wording, not the meaning of your content. You cannot get a model to recite a poem or chapter, but you can let it read every science journal and keep the knowledge. The least valuable part of what you publish is the part the law protects, she warns you about.

Oh, and what about your own prompts and file uploads to LLMs? In which you might reveal a lot of information about strategy and business ambitions? Your enterprise contract already keeps those out of the training runs, so we can ignore that concern. Maybe make sure your employees don't use their private chat gpt too much, for company purposes.

Here is the exposure that is actually left, and it is a subtle one. Imagine your are a retailer that builds its Google search bidding on an AI agent developed within Anthropics. No file that you upload can be accessed, or used for training. But the lab sees that this problem is worth solving, what a good answer looks like, and where its own model still falls short. Today that might be your competitive edge. And in two releases it is a feature your competitors can switch on. Satya Nadella described the mechanism: every time you use the tool and every time you correct it, the AI lab learns who you are. Your way of working comes back packaged in the next release, sold to everyone.

Figma, a leader in web design software, with revenue up nearly 50% in a year, lost more than three quarters of its IPO valuation. Anthropic shipped a capable free design tool, and the market concluded that what Figma does can be copied by a lab in no time. No files were stolen, all enterprise contracts were respected.

Karp's antidote to the exposure that is left, is to keep your ontology private. An ontology is he map of what your data means and how it connects. Sound advice, since without that ontology it is much harder to understand what you are building.

But he is leaving much out. Something still has to run on top of that map, an orchestration layer that sees everything, and in Palantir's world that layer is designed and built by Palantir. Keep your ontology away from the labs, and hand the whole picture to Palantir instead. Remember how companies rushed into SAP in the nineties, then watched their best practices reappear in SAP's catalogue.

And, not surprisingly, there is a remedy he never mentions. Run models whose weights you can control. Join the open weight model ecosystem. Download them, tune them on your own machines, and nothing leaves at all. No contract to trust, no learning loop to feed. Chinese DeepSeek and Moonshot have shipped open models that land within a few points of the frontier at something like a seventieth of the price, free to run on your own servers.

Which is what makes Palantir's second alarm, a week later, even more supsicious. Days after praising American open models, its technology chief warned that China's open models are stolen American intelligence and ought to be locked down. The logical solution for the value leakage to AI-labs, is now another risk.

Not consistent at all, these two warnings. Unless you look at them from Palantir's point of view. The labs move into enterprise software, threatening Palantir. So Karp attacks the labs that they drain your value. Fear of China will drive defence budgets, so Karp's CTO Sankar attacks Chinse models, and the AI-labs sloppy protection of their weights.

Nobody yet knows which stack will win over time. And that uncertainty is what you should remember. You need to protect now one thing: your ability to move. Hold your own ontology, keep the layer above it replaceable, keep the models underneath swappable. Take Karp's warning seriously. Just read it with his own interests subtracted, and keep your escape routes open.

Sources
Karp: enterprises are livid, the labs take your alpha
Alex Karp on CNBC · 1 July 2026

The alarm that opens the issue. On CNBC, Alex Karp accused the AI labs of draining value out of the enterprises that use them. His word for it was theft, and his examples were not about files: the labs, he argued, absorb the alpha, the way of working that makes a company win, through the very act of being used. The essay takes the warning seriously and then reads it with his interest subtracted, because Palantir sells the layer he recommends as the remedy. Watch the clip with both halves in mind. The mechanism he describes is real, and every version of the cure he offers happens to run through Palantir.

cnbc.com/2026/07/01/palantir-karp-open-ai-anthropic-tokens.html
Samuelson: copyright is a dead end for protecting your data
Pamela Samuelson on Lawfare's Scaling Laws podcast · July 2026

The legal ground under the essay's claim that the upload worry is settled. Pamela Samuelson, the Berkeley scholar who has shaped American copyright thinking for decades, walks through the AI copyright cases. Her core point: copyright protects the wording, and only the wording. Training counts largely as fair use when the material was obtained legally, the pirated-books cases end in settlements, and the meaning of what you publish, the knowledge itself, was never protected at all. A model can be barred from reciting your poem and still keep everything your poem taught it. For anyone hoping the law will guard their data position, she is the clearest voice explaining why it will not do that job.

lawfaremedia.org/article/scaling-laws--ai-copyright-lawsuits-with-pam-samuelson
Nadella: the moat is the learning loop, not the model
The Next Web · July 2026

Nadella supplies the mechanism behind Karp's anger. Even with training switched off by contract, the seller learns you as you use the tool: every prompt, every correction, every workflow shows the vendor which problem you are solving and what a good answer looks like. He calls it the reverse information paradox, the seller learning more about you than you learn about it, trace by trace. Coming from Microsoft's CEO the observation carries weight, since his company sits on more of those traces than anyone. It is the clearest statement of why protecting your data does not protect your position, which is the essay's central line.

thenextweb.com/news/nadella-reverse-information-paradox-ai-ip
Figma: value repriced overnight, no file stolen
The Motley Fool · 10 July 2026

The share price that proves the point. Figma, a healthy business with revenue up nearly half in a year, lost the bulk of its IPO valuation within months. No secret leaked and no contract was broken. What changed was belief: once Anthropic shipped a capable free design tool, the market concluded that what Figma does can be rebuilt by a lab in no time, and repriced the company accordingly. The Motley Fool piece walks through the numbers. The essay uses the case as the visible end of the mechanism Nadella describes: your edge can be copied out from above you, and the market does not wait for the copy to ship before it adjusts the price.

fool.com/investing/2026/07/10/why-figma-stock-lost-52-in-the-first-half-of-2026
Sankar: China's open models called stolen American IP
Shyam Sankar on Bloomberg · 15 July 2026

The second Palantir alarm, and the tell. Days after praising American open models, Palantir's technology chief warned on Bloomberg that China's open models amount to stolen American intelligence and ought to be locked down. Each warning makes sense read alone. Read together with Karp's, a pattern appears: the labs threaten Palantir's enterprise business, so the labs are the danger; fear of China lifts defence budgets, so China is the danger. The Chinese open models are today the most practical route to capable AI that feeds no American lab, and for Europe the shortest path to any sovereignty at all, which is exactly the route this warning talks down. The essay's advice: read the warning, subtract the interest.

bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-15/palantir-s-cto-sees-chinese-ai-models-posing-economic-risk-to-us
DeepSeek V4-Flash: near the frontier, at a seventieth of the price
DeepSeek, model release · 31 July 2026

The remedy Karp does not mention, priced. DeepSeek's V4-Flash lands within a few points of the frontier models at something like a seventieth of the price, and the weights are open: download them, tune them on your own machines, and nothing leaves your walls. No contract to trust, no learning loop to feed. The essay's escape route runs through exactly this class of model, which is what makes Sankar's warning above so interesting to read against it. Whether an open model is good enough for your workload is an empirical question, and the benchmark linked here is the place to start checking.

Issue #1  ·  31 Jul 2026

A model that frames its own thoughts

The safe thing to say about a language model is that it only predicts the next word. Then Anthropic found a small workspace inside Claude where it holds concepts it never says, and showed that swapping one changes everything downstream. This essay takes the finding seriously, and then asks the harder question: how much of the richness is the model's, and how much is ours, projected onto it.

Read this issue

On July 6th, Anthropic published a paper about the inner workings of Claude. To see why it caused a stir, it helps to recall how such a model works. A language model is layers of nodes, trained by tuning the connections between them until its predictions match the text it's shown. Once trained, it runs as a continuous stream: read what's been written, predict the next word, add it, repeat. There's no memory between conversations, and nothing we'd call a thought.

But the researchers found the model seems to hold concepts in mind that never appear in what it writes, stored in the 'J-space' (this is not a physical location, but a pattern spread across many nodes, identified with a mathematical tool called the Jacobian). When a concept is located there, those nodes light up far more than the rest.

An example: ask the model which currency is used in the country where the Eiffel Tower stands. To answer, it needs an intermediate step: the tower is in France, France uses the euro. So it tells you: euro, never mentioning France, since you didn't ask. Yet France is exactly what shows up in the J-space while the model works this out. Reach into the J-space and swap France for China, and the output changes accordingly.

Why is this special? Three things stand out: (1) the space is small, holding only a handful of concepts though nothing in the design demands that type of scarcity; (2) what's held there isn't being said, which is different from simply having a legible internal state; and (3), the special one: it is selective: some operations run through the space while others go around it. Together, that's more than most people expected a next-word predictor to do.

Neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene, who has long argued consciousness is essentially a shared internal workspace becoming available to the rest of the mind, found this thrilling: maybe that's simply what any system needs to think flexibly, machine or brain.

For what the J-space seems to do, Linguists would use the word 'framing'. And how it does that, echoes George Lakoff's Don't Think of an Elephant, on how the few concepts we hold active decide what we can say. Told not to think about a concept, the model half-obeyed, the forbidden idea showing up in the J-space more strongly than if it had never been raised.

Lakoff goes much further than Dehaene. He believes that concepts are inherently embodied: a frame like 'cat' can't be separated from the bodily, sensory experience that gives it meaning. That sounds reasonable to most of us. Reading that Claude is "holding" the concept of a cat, we fill in everything the word means to us, warmth, weight in the lap, a whole cloud of sensation, and conclude something rich must be happening inside. There's no reason to believe that. For the model, cat is just a position in a web of words, close to purr and whiskers, far from carburetor. The richness is ours, projected onto Claude.

But. Strip the projection away, and what's left is still framing. That narrower version has real pedigree: a century ago, linguist Ferdinand de Saussure argued that words mean what they mean through their place among other words, not by pointing at things in the world. It is funny to see that this forgotten theory tells us exactly how meaning works in LLMs.

So the J-space is a step, and a real one. The model does more than we thought a next-word predictor would: it holds concepts apart from its own speech and lets them shape what follows. What it offers is a glimpse of how much can be done with words alone: a great deal more than we assumed, and a great deal less than we are tempted to imagine.

Sources
Anthropic: Concepts held, and not spoken
A global workspace in language models · July 2026

On July 6th Anthropic published a paper that drew a great deal of attention, which I guess was deserved. Claude turns out to hold concepts somewhere in its middle layers that shape what it goes on to say, while those concepts themselves are never said. That somewhere is not a real place. It is a pattern spread across many nodes, brought to the surface with a piece of mathematics called the Jacobian, hence: 'J-space'. The authors are bold in one direction and careful in another. They borrow the vocabulary of neuroscience: an opening section on conscious access, and five properties to distinguish the thoughts we can get at from processing we never notice. Claude, they find, has all five. But access consciousness is a functional notion, a matter of what is available for reasoning and report, and on the separate question of whether anything is experienced, they state plainly that they take no position. The philosophical implications, they write, are unclear and likely controversial. Yet, our take is that it does seem like a kind of breakthrough. Most unique is that the space is very small, with only a handful of concepts. Second, its contents are withheld rather than spoken. And third, it is selective, with some operations running through it and others going around. Together that is more than a next-word predictor was supposed to manage.

anthropic.com/research/global-workspace
Dehaene & Naccache: Access to the workspace is what we call consciousness
Does Claude possess a conscious global workspace? · July 2026

When Anthropic invited outside experts to comment, they went to the people whose theory they had borrowed. Stanislas Dehaene, a cognitive neuroscientist at the Collège de France, and Lionel Naccache, a neurologist at the Paris Brain Institute, built the global neuronal workspace model together with the neurobiologist Jean-Pierre Changeux. It is among the most influential accounts of consciousness in neuroscience, and among the most deflationary: no inner light, no additional ingredient, nothing a machine could not have. They are the finding's intellectual parents, and they respond accordingly. They call it a landmark, chiefly because nobody installed the workspace. It emerged. They also point out the limitations. Claude has no 'ignition', i.e. the sudden all-or-nothing threshold that marks conscious access in humans. No body. No episodic memory. No continuity of self. It is hard to imagine, they write, what it would be like to be conscious for the length of a single conversation, and then switch off. On qualia (a common concept in philosophy not about objective properties, but subjective experience) they are merciless. Push the intuition hard enough and you find a hidden dualism.

unicog.org
George Lakoff: A frame cannot be switched off
Don't Think of an Elephant! · 2004

Among the experiments in the Anthropic paper is one in which the researchers instruct Claude not to think about something, and then check whether it obeys. It half obeys. The forbidden concept shows up in the J-space less strongly than when the model is told to hold it in mind, and far more strongly than when nobody raised it at all. In another experiment the model is told a thought may have been planted in it, and asked what it detects. Its own first guess, which nobody suggested, is 'elephant'. Anyone with a background in philosophy or linguistics will then immediately think of a book by George Lakoff: 'Don't think of an elephant!'. George Lakoff, a cognitive linguist at Berkeley, broke with his teacher Noam Chomsky over whether syntax runs on its own, indifferent to what words mean. He argued that it cannot. Every word summons a frame, a structure of expectation, image and feeling, and no frame is cancelled by putting "not" in front of it. Nixon told the country he was not a crook, so the country saw a crook. For Lakoff, a frame reaches into the body: into metaphor, memory, the felt sense of a thing. Which raises a question he never had to answer, because in 2004 only humans could frame.

george-lakoff.com/writings
Zellig Harris: The method that became the machine
Distributional Structure · 1954

The oldest text here is the one that reads most like a description of current technology. In 1954 Zellig Harris, a linguist at the University of Pennsylvania, proposed that a language can be analysed by tracking which words occur near which others, and that its structure will fall out of that distribution alone, with no appeal to what any word refers to. It was a proposal about method, written for linguists working with index cards. Seventy years later it is, in outline, how a language model is trained. The machine rests on a theory of meaning that its builders never needed to believe, or even to have read. The lineage is quarrelsome. Harris taught Noam Chomsky, who spent a career arguing that his teacher's method could never be enough. Lakoff then broke with Chomsky, and in doing so landed further from Harris than either of them: where Harris set the question of meaning aside, Lakoff put it back and put it in the body. The British linguist J.R. Firth said it best: you shall know a word by the company it keeps.

About

The Hedgehog & The Fox

We enjoy a good, firm argument about almost anything. Usually we end up converging, at a slightly higher level. Our interest in AI is large, but we approach it from very different sides: Martin from his expertise in analytics and big data, Ebel from the philosophy of language. What we share in experience is seeing up close what the adoption of AI demands of fast-growing digital native organisations.

In The Hedgehog & The Fox we bring our thinking on AI together. Each week we take one concept or one received opinion to task, guided by leading publications (so not the tweets of tech bros), and merge those ideas into a single essay. In that work, the I interests us more than the A. How must a complex system be organised to become intelligent, or more intelligent?

We do not claim to know where AI is heading, but we would gladly move the quality of the discussion forward. The least you may expect is to come away confused at a higher level.

Martin & Ebel

Martin Heijnsbroek
I · The Hedgehog

Entrepreneur, board advisor in AI, and hard to stop once he starts calculating. Built Singapore Telecom's first customer database with his own hands, won McKinsey's global knowledge prize. Spent seventeen years advising boards on data strategies, well before AI became a boardroom word, and has two private equity exits under his belt. Taught Amsterdam UvA students for ten years how to drive impact from AI, wrote columns for the FD, while he built rewirenow.com as a leading AI services company.

Today he leads the Data & AI agenda of Sani Ikos Group, advises HomeDAO in Oxford and rewirenow.com, while he remains a crypto enthusiast, whatever the charts say. Can be more convincing than he is convinced, a dangerous trait for readers and friends. Only works with people he enjoys, is a big fan of Greece, and met Ebel at Insead auditorium, shooting at a simplistic bathtub metaphor.

EK
Ebel Kemeling
II · The Fox

Two decades across finance, technology investment and organisational design, working on the economics of intelligence long before it was a headline. Writes on where value accrues, which frictions break first, and how the firm rearranges when computation is plentiful and judgment is scarce.

TH&TF Manifesto

Turning the cards

Artificial intelligence is not new. It goes back to the 1930s and the mathematics of computation. The war accelerated everything, and in the summer of 1956 the term Artificial Intelligence was coined. What followed became a seasonal rhythm. Extraordinary optimism, disillusionment, recovery. But since the early 1990s, the only way was up. Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997. Deep learning remade computer vision in 2012. AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in 2016. Huge breakthroughs, but not very visible to the public.

Enter ChatGPT in November 2022. Within two months, a hundred million people were using it. For the first time, AI was something anyone could use, every day. The technology had not suddenly changed. It had become visible. Plus, the richest people on earth placed enormous bets on it, the largest companies reorganized around it, and valuations reached gargantuan levels. Silicon Valley's marketing machine began pushing a story: this is the most important technology ever built, it will change everything, the only question is how fast.

That story frames how we privately speak about AI. But it is not always clear how. In our conversations, we use what cognitive scientists call chunks: ideas repeated so often they compress into a card you can play without checking what it refers to. Hybrid systems always work better. AI is ultimately a human matter. Every job will disappear. Machines cannot be creative. The cards get passed around and get nods of approval, without checking what it actually means, or if the person using the card has any idea what he is talking about.

These cards do not deal themselves. Nearly every card is dealt by a company that has an interest in you playing it. Anthropic says its models are too dangerous to share. OpenAI says it will drive the growth that pays for everything. Palantir warns against Chinese models. We are not clairvoyant, so we will not try to settle the matter. The best response is neither to believe them nor to dismiss them, but to take the arguments seriously, and understand them better than the people or companies using them.

Under all the cards hides the essence of the game we are playing: the understanding of what intelligence really is. Mostly we picture intelligence as a quality of a human brain. So the goal of AI, or even AGI, becomes to create an "Einstein in your pocket". But we also speak of smart teams, smart organizations, even smart cities and societies, and nobody thinks a city has a skull. So isn't intelligence a bit more than symbol manipulation inside a brain?

This is a platform for people who would rather think about AI than talk about it. The hedgehog and the fox, borrowed from Isaiah Berlin, are two strategies to approach a question. The hedgehog knows one big thing and follows it all the way down. The fox knows many things, circles around the question and keeps finding new angles. We use both, not to reach final answers, but to turn the cards over, one chunk, one thinker, one idea each week, and we try to uncover what it is about. You will be left not with conclusions, but hopefully will be a bit harder to sell to, and a bit better at asking the right questions.

This week: Karp's alarm about this level up, the remedy he does not mention, and why every warning Palantir sends out happens to sell a Palantir product.

Issue #1 · A model that frames its own thoughts
31 Jul 2026

The safe thing to say about a language model is that it only predicts the next word. Then Anthropic found a small workspace inside Claude where it holds concepts it never says, and showed that swapping one changes everything downstream. This essay takes the finding seriously, and then asks the harder question: how much of the richness is the model's, and how much is ours, projected onto it.
